newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan-Motorola phone row said resolved.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan-Motorola phone row said resolved.

text.p: Pakistan has resolved a dispute with Motorola Inc of the United States to allow it to resume cellular telephone services in troubled Karachi, U.S. Assistant Secretary of Commerce Raymond Vickery said on Saturday.
"I believe the matter has been resolved," he told a news conference after three days of talks with Pakistani officials and business representatives.
No Pakistani comment was immediately available as government offices were closed for the weekend.

Vickery said his understanding was that Motorola's Pakistani joint venture, Pakistan Mobile Telecommunications (Pvt) Ltd (PMCL), known locally as Mobilink, would soon resume services in the port city of Karachi, Pakistan's commercial hub, along with other cellular telephone companies.
But he said he did not know exactly when the services would be resumed.

Islamabad had cut off Mobilink from the state telephone network in Karachi in January last year, fearing the Motorola-made cellular telephones were more helpful to militants engaged in political violence there than other such sets.

Later in July last year, the government suspended operations of all cellular, payphone and pager companies in Karachi as it stepped up its crackdown against violence and the ban still continues, although violence has died down for several months.
Vickery said the ban on Motorola had been a matter of great concern for the United States although the action had been taken for security concerns.
He said he believed Motorola had been responsive to "these concerns".

Pakistani government officials had apparently feared that groups involved in political violence or crimes would use Mobilink cellular phones, which scramble communications by jumping frequencies at random, to avoid eavesdropping by intelligence agencies.

Last year, Mobilink was asked by authorities to provide what it called technical interfaces or capabilities that could enable authorities to scan and eavesdrop on over-the-air cellular calls made by customers.
It was not immediately known whether Mobilink had met these demands.
Last month, the government asked three cellular telephone companies to provide data on clients in what industry sources saw as a prelude to lifting the ban on mobile phones in Karachi.
More than 2,000 people were killed in political violence in Karachi last year, but the unrest has subsided this year, with the death toll standing at about 350 after eight months.
The three cellular telephone companies, a pager company and three telephone card companies say Karachi, home to 40 percent of their subscribers, is vital to their business in Pakistan.
